It did not consciously recognize the category of “negativity,” but in practice it understood things as though this category were present in them.

Magic did not believe that the “essence” of a thing remained eternally unchanged—or, what comes to the same thing, that the essence was always and everywhere determined by one and the same, “identical,” set of essential qualities.
For magic, a cat is not absolutely and permanently a cat. It can become a snake, a mountain, a human being, and so on.

This capacity to change essentially, to become independent of one’s “natural” place in the world—or, what comes to the same thing, this freedom and creative power of mana—is precisely what made mana seem “divine,” meaning supernatural, in the eyes of magic.
But this also meant that there could be no general, eternal, and immutable “laws” of magic.

Every individual case required its own particular “formula.” For magic to work, particular conditions had to be present, together with the intervention of a specially gifted individual: the “magician.”
Magic therefore had the character of an art, not of a “science” in the modern sense.
The Greek discovery that made science possible consisted, so to speak, in realizing that a cat is always, everywhere, and only a cat.
The Greeks saw that the “essence” of things is eternally immutable or “identical.”
A mountain is always a mountain; a cat is always a cat.
These things cannot turn or “metamorphose” into one another.
Every “essence” is completely determined by a precise set of “essential” qualities, and knowledge of these qualities gives anyone, anywhere, always power over the thing.
Essence therefore ceased to be something “divine” and became something belonging to physical nature.
Knowledge of essence ceased to be a “magical art” and became an ordinary, universally valid science.
Having made this discovery, the Greeks extended it to everything, including their “gods” and human beings themselves.
From then until Hegel, the category of identity remained the foundation of virtually all thinking about what exists: scientific, philosophical, and especially ontological.
There was, however, one exception: the biblical Hebrews and their monotheism.
Like the Greeks, and indeed like all peoples, the Hebrews passed through a “magical” stage.
The Greeks escaped from magic by, so to speak, fixing mana in place: dividing it into separate parts and attaching each part to a determinate thing with an eternal “nature.”
The Hebrews overcame magic by moving, so to speak, in the opposite direction.
They unified mana—which in magic had been both one and many—and moved this single, unified mana beyond the limits of every particular thing, and therefore beyond the world.
They called this single and super-natural mana God, or Yahweh.
The final picture was roughly this.
In God-as-mana, negativity predominates. God is a free and creative being.
The natural world has no independent “essence” of its own and therefore depends completely on the “free will” of the divine mana.
Human beings, meanwhile, are created “in the image and likeness of God,” meaning that they too are dialectical.
But they too depend on God, although differently from the natural world.
The natural world is therefore supposed to “serve” humanity insofar as humanity itself “serves” God.
Science obviously could not grow on such ground.
The natural world had no “essence” of its own, and therefore no scientific knowledge of it was possible.
There were no fixed “essences” determining things and no “immutable laws of nature.”
Everything was governed by divine arbitrariness, which could not be predicted.
At most, one could talk about the world by relating it to human beings and human purposes.
This produced “anthropocentrism” and “theologism”: the sun exists so that human beings can have light and warmth; it can even stop in its course so that the Jews can win a battle, and so on.
Human existence, for its part, is not governed by fixed laws belonging to human “nature.” It is governed by divine laws, meaning the free will of God-as-mana.
But knowledge of them is given by God through revelation, and God can change them through a “new revelation.”
The Scriptures therefore speak of religious laws, not of laws of nature.
To the extent that genuine and true knowledge was possible, it could not be a “science” of nature. It had to be theo-logy, a science of God.
When this Jewish religion encountered Greek philosophy in Christianity, an attempt was made to bring the two together.
The Greek, “scientific” category of identity was applied both to the Hebrew and “magical” God-as-mana, whose character was dialectical, and to the human being created in his likeness.
It is hardly surprising that the attempt failed.
Christian philosophy continually struggled with the resulting contradictions.
The attempt to reconcile “reason”—Greek science and philosophy based on the category of identity—with “faith”—the Jewish religion based on negativity—was no more successful.

Christian philosophy eventually admitted its failure by accepting, more or less openly, the doctrine of the so-called double truth: what is correct for “reason” need not be correct for “faith,” and vice versa.
Hegel’s “discovery,” one might say, consisted in preserving the Judeo-Christian, “dialectical” conception of the human being while eliminating the concept of God.
In one sense, Hegelianism is simply an atheistic Judeo-Christianity.
Hegel transferred to the human being everything that Judeo-Christianity had attributed to God.
Humanity became the free creator of itself and of its world.
The laws governing human life, like the “laws of nature,” are conditioned by human “essence.” Human beings prescribe these laws to themselves and can themselves change them.
In other words, like a “magical” thing, the human being can change his form.
The “Hegelian” human being does not depend on the natural world, and in this respect differs from the “Greek” human being.
But neither does he depend on God, and in this respect he differs from the “Judeo-Christian” human being.
This conception of humanity passed from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.
But, as I have already said, Hegel corrected the Greeks only to fall into the opposite error.
The Greeks understood human beings non-dialectically, in the image and likeness of natural things.
Hegel, by contrast, understood the natural world itself dialectically, in the image and likeness of human beings.
Instead of producing a synthesis of Greek Cosmology and Judeo-Christian anthropology—after first purifying the latter of theism—he effectively returned to a magical view of the world.
This is, indeed, exactly what happened in his Naturphilosophie, which is “magical” in the literal sense.
192) Hegel applies all three dialectical laws to every concept and every entity because he considers all being dialectical.

I, by contrast, hold that the classical logical laws apply to non-dialectical natural being, while the “positive” law of contradiction and the law of the included middle occur only in human beings, that is, in dialectical existence.
The “law of identity” applies to both kinds of being.
But in non-dialectical beings it applies to the whole thing.
In dialectical beings, by contrast, it applies only to the being taken as a thesis—that is, to the first stage of the dialectical process.

193) Once we seriously take human finitude into account—a finitude usually denied by philosophers who believe in human immortality, and all too rarely grasped in its full significance even by those who know that human beings are mortal—we have to admit that this is far from obvious.
But discussing the problem would take us too far.

I will say only that all traditional pre-Hegelian philosophy related logic, more or less openly and consciously, to divine reason—that is, to an infinite reason, infinite because eternal and outside time.
194) Hegel was mistaken in believing the opposite.
This error also led him to his mistaken dialectical monism: the claim that every kind of being whatsoever is dialectical.
195) I chose the term snjatie, snimat’, and so on.
First, because it is one possible literal translation of the German Aufheben: “to take off [snimat’] the lid of a saucepan.”
Second, because, if one wishes, the Russian word can also be made to carry the three “dialectical” meanings of the German term:
snjat’ in the sense of “remove from [snjat’] the repertoire”;
snjat’ in the sense of “take [snjat’] a photograph,” meaning to capture and in some sense preserve;
snjat’ in the expression snjat’ slivki, “skim off the cream,” meaning to retain and select what is best, most valuable, or “highest.”
196) A “primitive” culture is, in this sense, “lower” than ours because we can understand it.
Its representatives, by contrast, cannot understand our culture insofar as they rely only on what is given within their own culture and do not “enter” ours.
One outward sign of this is the relative poverty of a language.
To translate into Turkmen every book written, say, in Russian, it would be necessary to invent a great many new words.
By contrast, the existing vocabulary of Russian is sufficient to translate anything a Turkmen is capable of writing.
More generally, we can say that B is “higher” than A only when B includes A plus something more.
This is why a synthesis is higher than “its” thesis: it contains both that thesis and the antithesis.
197) Hegel speaks so formally and abstractly in these paragraphs because he wants to give definitions that apply equally to natural existence and to human—or, as he calls it, “spiritual”—existence.
Since I believe that dialectic occurs only in human beings, I could define it from the outset in less abstract terms than Hegel does.
Even on my own interpretation, however, we can distinguish the formal structure of dialectic from its concrete content by identifying what is common to all its manifestations.
We must also distinguish the ontological, cosmological, and phenomenological aspects of dialectic.
But a full treatment of this problem would take us too far.
I will say only that the formal definitions that follow are ontological, whereas the later remarks on dialectic as human existence will be cosmological.

As for the phenomenological aspect, that will be described in the text of the Phenomenology itself, which is nothing other than the in-principle complete description of real or concrete dialectic from the phenomenological point of view.
